metadata.note: The Denver & Rio Grande's original gateway into the San Luis Valley: Walsenburg over the Sangre de Cristo range to Alamosa, opened 1877-78 as the first leg of what became the San Juan Extension network (Antonito-Chama-Durango, covered by other layers in this dataset). RESEARCH FINDING ON THE 'DEPOT ABANDONED BY 1899' LEAD: this was not a mere station closure -- the D&RG built and ran an entirely new, physically distinct standard-gauge alignment in 1899 when it converted the pass crossing from narrow to standard gauge. The original line (crossed 1877, through service to Alamosa from July 6 1878) went north out of La Veta over what is now called Old La Veta Pass (9,380 ft), a summit with two tight curves on its eastern approach, then down Sangre de Cristo Creek to Russell and Fort Garland -- the original La Veta Pass depot (now a preserved building in the town of La Veta) served this line for about 20 years before being superseded in 1899. The 1899 realignment diverged from the old route just west of La Veta, climbed Middle Creek to a new, lower summit about 7-9 miles away (elevation reported as 9,220-9,242 ft depending on source; also called simply 'Veta Pass'), and descended via Wagon Creek, rejoining the original alignment just below Russell. Both alignments are drawn here as geometrically distinct features per CLAUDE.md Rule 2: a pre-1899 feature over the original pass, and a post-1899 feature over the new pass (itself split at the 1921 D&RG-to-D&RGW reorganization per Rule 4). Passenger service on the post-1899 line lasted into the early 1950s, latterly as a Pueblo-Alamosa connecting train ('The San Luis', trains 15/16) meeting the narrow-gauge San Juan to Durango at Alamosa; the exact final year (1951 vs 1953) is a source conflict, see not_yet_sourced. Not drawn here: the Rio Grande Scenic Railroad's 2006-2019 tourist excursions between Alamosa and La Veta over this same corridor (it went into receivership in 2019) -- a tourist_rail feature for that operation would be a reasonable future addition but is out of scope for this pass.

geometry_sources: Post-1899 (new/standard-gauge) alignment: real-traced from OpenStreetMap via Overpass, following railway=rail ways tagged operator=SLRG (San Luis & Rio Grande, the modern short-line operator) or Union Pacific Railroad with old_railway_operator=D&RGW, stitched Walsenburg-Alamosa with a haversine Dijkstra shortest path over a graph of way endpoints snapped to 5 decimal places. 1387 points, 123.4 km (76.7 mi) traced vs. 70.1 mi documented for this route (drgw.net, post-1937 figure) -- ratio ~1.09, consistent with real curvature on a mountain grade rather than a route-mileage figure. This is the same physical corridor still in freight use today.

Pre-1899 (original narrow-gauge) alignment: real-traced from OpenStreetMap via Overpass for the La Veta-to-Russell mountain crossing itself (railway=abandoned ways tagged old_railway_operator=D&RGW, a well-preserved abandoned grade largely corresponding to today's County Road 443 and County Road W.8 over Old La Veta Pass), spliced onto the same post-1899 geometry for the shared, unchanged Walsenburg-La Veta and Russell-Alamosa portions (per drgw.net, the two alignments only differ between La Veta and a point just below Russell). 856 points, 119.9 km (74.5 mi) total; no separate documented mileage was found for the original crossing alone to compare against.
not_yet_sourced: Exact end year of passenger service on this line is a source conflict: one search result (citing the December 1951 Official Guide of the Railways) describes a full Pueblo-La Veta-Alamosa timetable for train #15/#16 in December 1951 and states the route 'was last served by regularly scheduled passenger service in 1951'; a different search synthesis (citing coloradocentralmagazine.com's '40 years since the last All Aboard', which could not be directly fetched -- repeated ECONNRESET) states the same connector train, named 'The San Luis' from June 1 1951, remained in the timetable until June 2 1953. This file uses 1953 as the drawn end year (the more specific, later-sourced claim) but the conflict is unresolved -- if it is later confirmed that 1951 is correct, the final segment's end year should be trimmed back two years.
Frequency/headway for the 1878-1899 narrow-gauge era and the 1899-1921 standard-gauge D&RG era is not sourced from a real timetable anywhere in the research for this file; both are rough estimates.

The exact opening date of the very first trackage out of Walsenburg (vs. the pass crossing in 1877 and through service to Alamosa on July 6 1878) is not pinned down; 1878 is used as the drawn start year for through Walsenburg-Alamosa passenger service.

Whether any passenger service ran on this corridor between the 1953 (or 1951) end of regular service and the 2006 start of the Rio Grande Scenic Railroad's tourist excursions (not drawn on this layer) is not researched here.

properties.line: Denver & Rio Grande: Walsenburg – Alamosa (Old La Veta Pass)
properties.speed_source: estimated: 3-foot narrow gauge with reported 4% grades and sharp curves climbing to a 9,380 ft summit -- among the steepest and slowest mainline mountain crossings D&RG operated; unsourced, no period timetable found

segments.note: William Jackson Palmer's Denver & Rio Grande pushed the narrow-gauge San Juan Extension west from Walsenburg over La Veta Pass -- at 9,380 ft the highest pass on any US railroad at the time -- crossing the summit in 1877 and reaching the new town of Alamosa on July 6 1878 (the line continued on to Antonito in 1878, the gateway to the Cumbres Pass route toward Durango, covered elsewhere in this dataset). This alignment ran north out of La Veta, over the pass, then down Sangre de Cristo Creek through Russell to Fort Garland and on to Alamosa. The pass's original depot (still standing in La Veta) served this line for about 20 years. Superseded in 1899 by a new, physically distinct standard-gauge alignment over a different, lower summit a few miles away -- see the companion features on this layer. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.line: Denver & Rio Grande: Walsenburg – Alamosa (La Veta Pass)
properties.speed_source: estimated: standard-gauge mountain grade, lower and less curvy than the original narrow-gauge crossing but still climbing to over 9,200 ft; unsourced, no period timetable found for this specific era

segments.note: The D&RG converted the La Veta Pass crossing from narrow to standard gauge in 1899, building an entirely new alignment: diverging from the old narrow-gauge route just west of La Veta, climbing Middle Creek to a new summit about 7-9 miles from (and roughly 100-150 ft lower than) the original Old La Veta Pass, then descending via Wagon Creek to rejoin the original alignment just below Russell. The old narrow-gauge segment between Russell and La Veta was largely torn up in 1901. This new crossing is commonly just called 'Veta Pass' or 'La Veta Pass' interchangeably in sources. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.line: Denver and Rio Grande Western: Walsenburg – Alamosa (La Veta Pass)
properties.speed_source: estimated: standard-gauge mountain grade, lower and less curvy than the original narrow-gauge crossing but still climbing to over 9,200 ft; unsourced, no period timetable found for this specific era

segments.note: The Denver & Rio Grande Railway was reorganized as the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad, which formally took over July 31 1921 after a bankruptcy in which the old company's stockholders received nothing -- a genuine change of ownership, not just a renaming. Under D&RGW this route carried standard-gauge trains connecting Pueblo/Walsenburg with Alamosa, where passengers could change to the narrow-gauge San Juan Express to Durango (which itself ran Feb 11 1937-Jan 31 1951 via Cumbres Pass, a different route covered elsewhere in this dataset). By December 1951 the connecting service was train #15/#16 ('The San Luis'), calling at La Veta and Fir before reaching Alamosa. Regular passenger service on this route ended in the early 1950s -- sources conflict on the exact year (1951 vs 1953); see not_yet_sourced.
